extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in mass communication and media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks, criteria, and methodological guidance for studying patterns and effects of mass media content (especially television, newspapers, and magazines), including quantitative vs qualitative approaches, models of media influence, bias typologies, and measures such as frequency and prominence compared to reality benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative v. Qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral content analysis tends to be quantitative (numerical); humanistic content study gravitates toward qualitative analysis. Berelson (1952) defines content analysis as the 'objective, systematic, quantitative and manifest analysis of content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantification is valuable for summarizing what is found and for comparing media content to reality benchmarks (e.g., percent of Latinos shown on TV vs percent in population), but reducing text to numbers 'does not provide a complete picture of meaning and contextual codes,' since texts contain many other forms of emphasis besides repetition (Gitlin, 1980). Use qualitative methods to recover meaning and contextual codes; use quantitative methods to measure frequency/patterns and enable comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare content to reality benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing how frequently things, people, and places appear in media content allows comparison of media content to some reality benchmark (e.g., percent of Latinos on prime-time TV versus percent in U.S. population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If we know content patterns, we can try to understand them by examining the organizations and people behind them. Choose appropriate external benchmarks (census, police reports, observed events) and be cautious about which benchmark is relevant to the research question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for systematic, repetitive patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers are drawn to repetitive patterns of widely attended-to mediated messages that have social significance and were produced by media organizations in a routine and standardized way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic repetitive patterns make it more likely that content represents an underlying cultural pattern or organizational logic. Prioritize content that is routine and standardized over isolated idiosyncratic items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive role: Media as channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Some conceptions view media as passive transmitters or channels—'pipes or conduits' through which bits of information flow—implying that nothing important happens to the message while it is in the channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this model (e.g., Lasswell; Westley & MacLean), effects on audiences are due to source or audience characteristics, not to transformations carried out by the media. When analyzing content, consider whether the research assumes nonpurposive transmission and test implications accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral journalist assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic profession's claim that reporters 'do not make the news; we report it'—the ideal of a disinterested, independent observer who presents events 'from nobody's point of view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using this assumption, beware that it may obscure structural practices (selection, headlines, framing) that signify importance. Examine journalistic conventions (headlines, access, soundbites) that perform selection/evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null effects / representative content model
rubrics_metrics.description: The null effects model holds mass media provide a fair representation of reality with little or no distortion; Young argues representative content results from counterbalancing forces (e.g., market pressures) rather than journalist neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of representativeness by assessing whether market/countervailing influences plausibly limit distortion. Test by comparing outlets and by checking for distortions that would reduce audience/lucrativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active role: Media as participants (manipulating reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media can impose their own structure and logic on events in creating a media world—singling out and highlighting certain elements over others, emphasizing behaviors and people, stereotyping, and relocating events into stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine selection, emphasis (time, prominence), stereotyping, rhetorical labels (e.g., 'freedom fighter' vs 'terrorist'), and how reassembly of event materials structures symbolic environment. Focus on prominence measures (time, placement) and rhetorical framing as evidence of media construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual v. verbal manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual content can be manipulated through cropping, camera angles, shot selection, perspective, slow motion, and juxtaposition—images are not inherently more 'direct' than text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include analysis of photographs, video shot selection, camera perspective (eye-level vs low/high), and editing/graphics (e.g., superimposed images, on-screen marks) as part of content analysis. Use examples (Gitlin; Kepplinger; Televisa; CBS 'x' graphic; Murrow's juxtaposition) to illustrate visual manipulation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection bestows importance (newsworthiness selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of topics, stories, or parts of events is itself an act that bestows importance (Wright's view of correlation as 'selection, evaluation and interpretation of events').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying media content, analyze not only what is present but what is omitted; investigate conventions (headlines, lead placement, visuals) that signal relative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on major mass media and widely shared content
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass communication studies traditionally focus on mediated content widely shared by a large audience—primarily television, newspapers, and magazines—rather than small-scale media (memos, cassette recordings, bulletin boards) or less central media (books, billboards, records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit samples to major channels when the research question targets mass shared symbolic environments; explicitly justify exclusions and note limits to generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer systematic, representative studies over idiosyncratic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Select studies that describe patterns of media content rather than coverage of a single story or issue; prefer the systematic over the idiosyncratic and include comparisons to social reality benchmarks where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design content analyses to capture patterns across time/space and across comparable units; avoid drawing generalizations from single-event case studies unless specifically contextualized.

rubrics_metrics.name: McQuail's typology of news bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias defined as 'a consistent tendency to depart from the straight path of objective truth'—McQuail proposes four types of news bias by openness and intent: partisanship (open/intended), propaganda (hidden/intended), unwitting bias (open/unintended), and ideology (hidden/unintended, 'embedded in texts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed bias along the openness/intention axes. Recognize that ideology (hidden/unintended) is difficult to demonstrate with simple content enumeration and may require deeper textual or contextual analysis; propaganda may be found in PR-derived materials and disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring bias: caution about simplistic quantitative balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures (column inches, seconds of airtime) are commonly used to assess balance, but they can be misleading because events drive news and selection is not necessarily representative of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume quantitative parity equals fairness; consider event incidence, editorial selection processes, and qualitative aspects (tone, framing). Establish an acceptable standard of fairness or benchmark before claiming bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative measures across outlets and modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media channels and outlets can vary markedly in how they cover the same event; empirical comparisons (e.g., two newspapers in one town, eyewitness vs television viewers) can reveal media-imposed differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare coverage across outlets, modalities (live attendance vs television), or timeframes to identify discrepancies attributable to media processes (camera selection, editorial choice). Use matched observation designs (Langs' parade study) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions for behaviors (example: violence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define behaviors precisely for coding—for example, Gerbner defines violence as 'overt expression of physical force' and reports incidence measures (percent of shows with violence, violent acts per hour, percent of leading characters involved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear operational definitions for coded behaviors, report both incidence (percent of programs with X) and intensity (acts per hour, fatalities), and where possible compare media incidence to relevant real-world statistics to illustrate discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation requires multiple information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reality is constructed from many information sources (officials, eyewitnesses, newspapers, broadcasts, directories, internal documents); because no one source conveys the entire picture, differences among sources can indicate distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulate media content analysis with other sources (official records, eyewitness accounts, internal documents) to assess how media representations align or deviate from other pieces of social reality. Acknowledge limits due to inaccessible sources.
